newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Brunei-Singapore dollar peg beneficial - economists.
newsitem.headline: Brunei-Singapore dollar peg beneficial - economists.

text.p: Brunei's currency peg with the Singapore dollar provides the tiny oil kingdom with an anchor of stability it is unlikely to abandon even as it aims to diversify its export base, economists said on Tuesday.

They said Singapore and Brunei's joint denial on Monday of market rumours they were planning to de-link their currencies confirmed that neither country would want to withdraw from an agreement that benefits both.

The statement gave added impetus to the Singapore dollar's sharp rise on Monday, which had already been triggered by comments by Singapore's Finance Minister Richard Hu about the currency maintaining its more modest rise of recent years, forex dealers said.

"There have been rumours of de-linking on and off for over a year and the last statement from Brunei on the desire to diversify its economy would have thrown the currency question into the open again," said Alex Erskine, regional market strategist with Citibank.

Speculation of a de-linking, which first surfaced last July, re-emerged in late February after Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah announced a five-year BR$7.2 billion development plan aimed at diversifying the economy by boosting non-oil exports.
The sudden resignation of Brunei's Finance Minister, Jefri Bolkiah, days after the announcement fuelled the speculation.
A joint statement by the governments of Brunei and Singapore on Monday said the two countries had "no intention of terminating the currency interchangeability agreement".

Desmond Supple, chief economist for Asia-Pacific currencies at Barclays (BZW), said the statement was positive for the Singapore dollar, which benefits from regular inflows of funds from Brunei companies repatriating their oil and gas export earnings.
"It's been a successful arrangement. It provides an anchor of stability to Brunei and also imposes Singapore's impressive inflationary discipline on the country," Supple said.
He said the currency peg also reduced Brunei's import costs and could therefore indirectly benefit its non-oil exports.
Citibank's Erskine said the arrangement placed the onus on Brunei authorities to "come up with non-exchange rate driven means of building depth in their economy".
